items.prompt: A function only needs to determine whether any value appears more than once. Which state is sufficient during a left-to-right scan?

options.text: A full frequency map is always required.
Only the immediately previous value.
A set of values seen so far.
An output array containing every processed value.

feedback.reason: Presence state is sufficient when the result depends only on whether a value appeared before.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “A set of values seen so far.” The scan checks whether the current value is already in the seen set. If it is, a duplicate exists; otherwise the value is inserted before moving on. Exact counts are unnecessary because the contract asks only for a yes-or-no answer.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Presence state is sufficient when the result depends only on whether a value appeared before.

items: A full frequency map is always required. — Counts would work, but they retain more information than the contract requires.
Only the immediately previous value. — A repeated value may be separated from its earlier occurrence in an unsorted input.
An output array containing every processed value. — Storing the processed prefix does not provide efficient membership state and retains unnecessary data.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_map_required: Counts would work, but they retain more information than the contract requires.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.previous_value_only: A repeated value may be separated from its earlier occurrence in an unsorted input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_array: Storing the processed prefix does not provide efficient membership state and retains unnecessary data.

items.prompt: A report must return the exact number of occurrences of every distinct value. Which state matches the contract?

options.text: A set recording whether each value appeared.
A mapping from each value to its current count.
One boolean indicating whether any duplicate exists.
One variable containing the previous input value.

feedback.reason: Exact multiplicity requires a count for each distinct value.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “A mapping from each value to its current count.” A frequency map distinguishes one occurrence from two, three, or more. Presence-only state collapses all positive counts into the same fact and therefore cannot reproduce exact frequencies.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Exact multiplicity requires a count for each distinct value.

items: A set recording whether each value appeared. — A set records presence but loses the number of occurrences.
One boolean indicating whether any duplicate exists. — One boolean cannot identify which values occurred or how often.
One variable containing the previous input value. — The previous value provides only local adjacency information, not global counts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.seen_set: A set records presence but loses the number of occurrences.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_flag: One boolean cannot identify which values occurred or how often.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.previous_value: The previous value provides only local adjacency information, not global counts.

items.prompt: A function must return the index of the first occurrence of every distinct value. Which mapping should it maintain?

options.text: Overwrite the stored index every time the value appears.
Map each value only to its total count.
Map each index to the value already stored at that index.
Map each value to its index only when that value is first encountered.

feedback.reason: The state update rule must preserve the first index rather than replace it.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “Map each value to its index only when that value is first encountered.” When a value is absent from the map, its current index becomes the first occurrence. Later occurrences must not overwrite that entry. A count alone does not preserve position.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The state update rule must preserve the first index rather than replace it.

items: Overwrite the stored index every time the value appears. — Overwriting implements a last-occurrence contract, not a first-occurrence contract.
Map each value only to its total count. — Counts do not identify where the first occurrence appeared.
Map each index to the value already stored at that index. — The input already provides index-to-value access; this mapping does not answer first-index queries efficiently.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value_to_latest_index: Overwriting implements a last-occurrence contract, not a first-occurrence contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value_to_count: Counts do not identify where the first occurrence appeared.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_to_value: The input already provides index-to-value access; this mapping does not answer first-index queries efficiently.

items.prompt: A function must return the index of the last occurrence of every distinct input value. Which update rule is correct during a left-to-right scan?

options.text: Store the index only when the value is first encountered.
Assign the current index to the value on every occurrence.
Increment the stored index by one on every occurrence.
Store only the number of occurrences.

feedback.reason: For a last-occurrence contract, each newer position must replace the older one.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “Assign the current index to the value on every occurrence.” After the full scan, the most recent assignment for each value is its final position. Write-once state would preserve the first occurrence instead.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: For a last-occurrence contract, each newer position must replace the older one.

items: Store the index only when the value is first encountered. — This retains the first index and ignores later occurrences.
Increment the stored index by one on every occurrence. — The next integer after an old index is not necessarily the position of the new occurrence.
Store only the number of occurrences. — A count does not identify the final position.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.write_only_when_absent: This retains the first index and ignores later occurrences.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.increment_index: The next integer after an old index is not necessarily the position of the new occurrence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_count_only: A count does not identify the final position.

items.prompt: The input consists only of lowercase English letters, and the algorithm needs exact character frequencies. Which state is the most direct?

options.text: A copy of every character processed so far.
One counter shared by all letters.
An array of 26 counters indexed by character.
Only the previous character.

feedback.reason: A small fixed domain supports direct indexed frequency state.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “An array of 26 counters indexed by character.” Each lowercase letter maps to one stable counter. The array size is independent of input length, so it is both simple and sufficient for exact frequencies.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: A small fixed domain supports direct indexed frequency state.

items: A copy of every character processed so far. — The full prefix contains the needed information but retains far more state than necessary.
One counter shared by all letters. — One counter cannot distinguish frequencies of different letters.
Only the previous character. — Local adjacency state cannot recover global character counts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_entire_prefix: The full prefix contains the needed information but retains far more state than necessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_counter: One counter cannot distinguish frequencies of different letters.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.previous_character: Local adjacency state cannot recover global character counts.

items.prompt: The input contains arbitrary 64-bit integers, and only values that actually occur should consume state. Which representation is appropriate for exact counts?

options.text: An array indexed directly by every possible 64-bit integer.
One boolean shared by all values.
A counter that resets whenever the current value differs from the previous one.
A hash map from encountered value to count.

feedback.reason: A sparse, very large value domain calls for state allocated only for encountered keys.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “A hash map from encountered value to count.” A hash map stores one entry per distinct observed value. Direct indexing over the full 64-bit domain is infeasible, while adjacent-run counting does not capture separated occurrences.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: A sparse, very large value domain calls for state allocated only for encountered keys.

items: An array indexed directly by every possible 64-bit integer. — The theoretical index range is far too large to allocate directly.
One boolean shared by all values. — One boolean cannot distinguish values or preserve exact counts.
A counter that resets whenever the current value differs from the previous one. — Separated occurrences of the same value would be counted as different runs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_by_numeric_value: The theoretical index range is far too large to allocate directly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.seen_boolean: One boolean cannot distinguish values or preserve exact counts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_count: Separated occurrences of the same value would be counted as different runs.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for detecting a repeated value while scanning an unsorted sequence with a seen set.

elements.text: Check whether the value is already in the seen set.
Report repetition if present; otherwise insert the value.

feedback.reason: Membership must be checked against prior state before the current occurrence is inserted.

blocks.text: The seen set represents values from earlier positions. On [4, 7, 4], the first 4 is absent and is inserted, 7 is absent and is inserted, and the final 4 is already present, so repetition is reported. Inserting before checking would make even the first 4 appear previously seen and would destroy the distinction between first and repeated occurrences.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Membership must be checked against prior state before the current occurrence is inserted.

items: Initialize the set before reading input so it represents an empty processed prefix.
Read one current value; the set still contains only earlier positions.
Check membership before mutating the set, preserving the distinction between first and later occurrences.
Report a hit immediately; on a miss, insert the value so later occurrences can be detected.

items.prompt: When is presence-only state sufficient? Select all that apply.

options.text: The decision depends only on whether the value appeared before.
The output must preserve the exact number of occurrences.
The output needs the set of distinct values but not their counts.
The output must return the first index of each value.

feedback.reason: Presence state is sufficient only when counts and positional metadata are irrelevant.

blocks.text: The correct choices are “The decision depends only on whether the value appeared before.” and “The output needs the set of distinct values but not their counts.” A set preserves membership. It can answer whether a value appeared and can represent the distinct values. It cannot recover exact multiplicity or occurrence positions.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Presence state is sufficient only when counts and positional metadata are irrelevant.

items: The output must preserve the exact number of occurrences. — Presence collapses every positive count into one state and loses exact multiplicity.
The output must return the first index of each value. — A set does not store the position of the first occurrence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.need_exact_multiplicity: Presence collapses every positive count into one state and loses exact multiplicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.need_first_index: A set does not store the position of the first occurrence.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.need_any_prior_occurrence: Prior membership is exactly the fact represented by a seen set.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.need_distinct_membership: A set directly represents which distinct values occur.

items.prompt: A left-to-right scan processes n values and stores one hash-map entry per distinct value. Select the expected time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: Hash lookup and update are expected O(1) per processed value.
d is the number of distinct input values.

feedback.reason: The algorithm performs one expected-constant update per input occurrence and retains one entry per distinct key.

blocks.text: Processing n values gives expected O(n) time. The map size follows d, not the number of loop statements. In the worst case d equals n, but O(d) states the tighter relationship.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: The algorithm performs one expected-constant update per input occurrence and retains one entry per distinct key.

items: time: O(n)
auxiliary space: O(d)
O(d) time ignores repeated input occurrences: d can be 1 while the scan still processes n values.
O(1) auxiliary space ignores the one retained entry for each of d distinct keys.
O(n log n) time would fit sorting or logarithmic updates, but the prompt grants expected O(1) hash operations per value.

items.prompt: A function must return all values that occur exactly once. Which state directly supports the required post-scan test?

options.text: Only a set of values that have appeared at least once.
A frequency count for each distinct value.
One boolean indicating whether any duplicate exists.
Only the immediately previous value.

feedback.reason: Selecting values with count exactly one requires distinguishing one occurrence from two or more.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “A frequency count for each distinct value.” A presence set cannot tell whether a value appeared once or repeatedly. Exact counts provide the post-scan predicate count[value] = 1. Full counts are a direct sufficient representation, although a deliberately compressed state that distinguishes zero, one, and at least two occurrences could also support this particular predicate.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Selecting values with count exactly one requires distinguishing one occurrence from two or more.

items: Only a set of values that have appeared at least once. — A normal seen set retains only whether a value ever appeared, not how many times.
One boolean indicating whether any duplicate exists. — A global flag cannot identify which particular values are unique.
Only the immediately previous value. — Separated occurrences would not be combined into one global count.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.seen_once_set: A normal seen set retains only whether a value ever appeared, not how many times.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_exists_flag: A global flag cannot identify which particular values are unique.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.previous_value_only: Separated occurrences would not be combined into one global count.

items.prompt: When is comparing only the current value with the previous value sufficient for duplicate-related reasoning?

options.text: For detecting all repeated values in any unsorted input.
For computing exact global frequencies of arbitrary values.
For returning the first index of every distinct value.
When the contract concerns consecutive runs, or equal values are guaranteed to be grouped.

feedback.reason: Previous-value state represents local adjacency, not global history.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “When the contract concerns consecutive runs, or equal values are guaranteed to be grouped.”. It is sufficient when only consecutive equality matters or when preprocessing guarantees that equal values form one run. Otherwise, separated occurrences require broader seen or frequency state.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Previous-value state represents local adjacency, not global history.

items: For detecting all repeated values in any unsorted input. — A repeated value can reappear after many unrelated values.
For computing exact global frequencies of arbitrary values. — Local run lengths do not combine separated occurrences without a grouping guarantee.
For returning the first index of every distinct value. — The previous value does not preserve the first index of every distinct key.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_unsorted_duplicates: A repeated value can reappear after many unrelated values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exact_global_counts: Local run lengths do not combine separated occurrences without a grouping guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_index_lookup: The previous value does not preserve the first index of every distinct key.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish presence state from frequency state? Select all that apply.

options.text: A set can answer whether a value has appeared.
A set directly preserves the exact count of every value.
A frequency map can distinguish one occurrence from several.
Either structure may grow with the number of distinct values.

feedback.reason: Presence and multiplicity are different information contracts, while both structures may scale with distinct keys.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “A set can answer whether a value has appeared.”, “A frequency map can distinguish one occurrence from several.”, “Either structure may grow with the number of distinct values.”. A set stores membership. A frequency map stores membership plus a count. Choosing between them should follow the information required by the result, not an assumption that one is always constant-space.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Presence and multiplicity are different information contracts, while both structures may scale with distinct keys.

items: A set directly preserves the exact count of every value. — A standard set records only whether a key is present.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.set_preserves_exact_counts: A standard set records only whether a key is present.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.set_answers_membership: Membership is the core fact represented by a set.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.map_preserves_multiplicity: The numeric value associated with each key preserves exact occurrence count.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.both_may_grow_with_keys: Both may contain one entry per distinct observed value.

items.prompt: Which statements describe a correct exact-frequency invariant during a left-to-right scan? Select all that apply.

options.text: After processing a prefix, count[x] equals the number of occurrences of x in that prefix.
Before a value is first seen, its logical count is zero.
The count of the previous value must reset whenever the current value changes.
Each processed occurrence increments exactly one counter once.

feedback.reason: Exact frequencies are maintained as cumulative counts over the processed prefix.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “After processing a prefix, count[x] equals the number of occurrences of x in that prefix.”, “Before a value is first seen, its logical count is zero.”, “Each processed occurrence increments exactly one counter once.”. A missing key represents zero earlier occurrences, and every new occurrence increases its own value's count once. Counts do not reset merely because another value appears.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Exact frequencies are maintained as cumulative counts over the processed prefix.

items: The count of the previous value must reset whenever the current value changes. — Resetting on value changes would count adjacent runs rather than global frequency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_on_change: Resetting on value changes would count adjacent runs rather than global frequency.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.processed_prefix_count: This is the central correctness invariant for the frequency table.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.missing_means_zero: Zero is the correct prior count before the first occurrence.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.increment_once: One occurrence contributes exactly one to its value's multiplicity.

items.prompt: An algorithm uses one loop but stores every distinct value encountered. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: One loop guarantees O(1) auxiliary space.
Any growing state makes the running time O(n²).
The running time may be linear, but auxiliary space can still grow with the distinct-value count.
All stored seen-state is automatically output space.

feedback.reason: Iteration count and retained memory are independent complexity dimensions.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “The running time may be linear, but auxiliary space can still grow with the distinct-value count.”. A single pass can perform O(n) expected work while keeping O(d) auxiliary state. The seen structure is auxiliary unless it is itself the required returned result.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Iteration count and retained memory are independent complexity dimensions.

items: One loop guarantees O(1) auxiliary space. — Loop count does not bound the size of a collection created inside the loop.
Any growing state makes the running time O(n²). — State growth does not imply that each operation scans all stored entries.
All stored seen-state is automatically output space. — Working memory and returned output must be classified according to their roles, not merely their contents.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_loop_constant_space: Loop count does not bound the size of a collection created inside the loop.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.growing_state_quadratic_time: State growth does not imply that each operation scans all stored entries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.state_is_output: Working memory and returned output must be classified according to their roles, not merely their contents.

items.prompt: What information is lost when a frequency map is replaced by a set? Select all that apply.

options.text: The exact count of each value.
Whether a value appears at all.
The ability to distinguish one occurrence from multiple occurrences.
Which distinct values appear.

feedback.reason: A set preserves keys but discards multiplicity.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “The exact count of each value.”, “The ability to distinguish one occurrence from multiple occurrences.”. Membership and the distinct-key collection remain available. What disappears is the numeric information needed to distinguish one, two, or more occurrences.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: A set preserves keys but discards multiplicity.

items: Whether a value appears at all. — Replacing a map entry with a set element keeps the key present; only its numeric count is discarded.
Which distinct values appear. — The elements of the set are the distinct keys.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.membership: Replacing a map entry with a set element keeps the key present; only its numeric count is discarded.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distinct_keys: The elements of the set are the distinct keys.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.exact_count: A set has no field that records the numeric frequency associated with a key.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.single_vs_multiple: Both one occurrence and many occurrences reduce to the same present state in a set.

items.prompt: An algorithm counts characters using an array of 26 integers while scanning a string of length n. Select the time and auxiliary-space complexity under the fixed lowercase-English-alphabet model.
constraints: The alphabet size is fixed at 26.
The result does not return the counter array.

feedback.reason: The scan grows with n, while the counter array has a fixed size independent of n.

blocks.text: Processing each character gives O(n) time. A 26-entry array is O(26), which is also O(1) asymptotically because the alphabet is fixed. Both accepted forms describe the same fixed-domain memory bound.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: The scan grows with n, while the counter array has a fixed size independent of n.

items: time: O(n)
auxiliary space: O(1) or O(26)
O(1) or O(26) time counts the fixed counter slots but ignores the scan of n input characters.
O(n log n) time would require sorting or logarithmic work per character; direct counter updates are constant time.
O(n) auxiliary space would apply if the state grew with the string, but the 26 counters stay fixed.

items.prompt: A task only asks whether every value occurs an even number of times. Which state can be sufficient without storing full counts?

options.text: A complete copy of the input sequence.
One parity bit or boolean per distinct value, toggled on each occurrence.
Only the immediately previous value.
One global parity bit shared by all values.

feedback.reason: The state should retain exactly the information required by the final predicate.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “One parity bit or boolean per distinct value, toggled on each occurrence.”. For an even-versus-odd decision, exact counts are unnecessary. Toggling one parity state per value preserves whether that value has appeared an odd or even number of times.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The state should retain exactly the information required by the final predicate.

items: A complete copy of the input sequence. — The full sequence retains far more information than the parity contract requires.
Only the immediately previous value. — Separated occurrences of the same value would not be combined.
One global parity bit shared by all values. — One global bit cannot distinguish the parity of different values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.full_input_copy: The full sequence retains far more information than the parity contract requires.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.previous_value: Separated occurrences of the same value would not be combined.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_parity: One global bit cannot distinguish the parity of different values.

items.prompt: Two strings contain lowercase English letters. The task is to determine whether they contain the same characters with the same multiplicities, while character order is irrelevant. Which approach matches the required state?

options.text: Compare only the sets of characters that appear.
Compare only the first character of each string.
Equal lengths alone prove equal multiplicities.
Build character-frequency arrays and compare all counters.

feedback.reason: Equal multiplicities require count state for every relevant character.

blocks.text: The correct choice is “Build character-frequency arrays and compare all counters.” Because order is irrelevant, positions need not be preserved. However, presence alone is insufficient: “aab” and “abb” have the same distinct characters and the same length but different counts. Comparing all 26 counters preserves and checks exactly the required multiplicities.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Equal multiplicities require count state for every relevant character.

items: Compare only the sets of characters that appear. — Sets cannot distinguish different multiplicities of the same characters.
Compare only the first character of each string. — The first position does not summarize the remaining characters or their counts.
Equal lengths alone prove equal multiplicities. — Equal total length does not imply that each character count matches.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_seen_sets: Sets cannot distinguish different multiplicities of the same characters.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_first_characters: The first position does not summarize the remaining characters or their counts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_lengths_only: Equal total length does not imply that each character count matches.

items.prompt: An algorithm scans n values from a domain of size R, updates an R-entry counter array, and then scans all R counters to find the most frequent value. Select its time, auxiliary-space, and output-space complexity.
constraints: The result is one value and one count.

feedback.reason: The algorithm traverses both the input and the counter domain, while the counters are temporary state.

blocks.text: Updating counts costs O(n), and finding the maximum across R counters costs O(R). The R counters are auxiliary space; returning one value and count is constant-size output.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: The algorithm traverses both the input and the counter domain, while the counters are temporary state.

items: time: O(n + R)
auxiliary space: O(R)
output space: O(1)
O(n) alone omits the required scan of all R counters when R is not fixed relative to n.
O(R) alone omits reading the n input values.
O(nR) multiplies two sequential scans that should be added, not treated as nested.
O(1) auxiliary space ignores the temporary R-entry counter array, while O(R) output space misclassifies that temporary array as the constant-size returned pair.

items.prompt: A function scans n values, builds a temporary frequency map with d keys, and returns a new array containing the k values whose frequency is exactly one. Select its expected time, auxiliary-space, and output-space complexity.

feedback.reason: The map stores one count per distinct key, while the returned array stores only qualifying values.

blocks.text: The input scan is expected O(n), and iterating over d map entries is O(d), which is bounded by n. The temporary map is O(d) auxiliary space, and the required result is O(k) output space.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: The map stores one count per distinct key, while the returned array stores only qualifying values.

items: time: O(n) or O(n + d)
auxiliary space: O(d)
output space: O(k)
O(1) time ignores both the n input values and the d map entries examined to form the result.
O(n log n) time would describe sorting or logarithmic updates, but expected O(1) hash updates are stated.
O(k) auxiliary space confuses the returned array with temporary state; the map retains d keys even when k is small.
O(d) output space overstates the required result when only k of the d distinct values occur exactly once.
